claims.source: Of these differentially expressed RNAs, 78% were increased in levels and 22% were decreased.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: The population of Rrp6-sensitive RNAs was considerably enriched in ncRNAs.
claims.source: The population of Rrp6-sensitive RNAs was considerably enriched in ncRNAs (p<0.001, Chi-square test) (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Approximately 43% of RNAs that accumulated in cut14-208 also accumulated in rrp6Δ cells.
claims.source: Pairwise comparison with cut14-208 revealed that ~ 43% (n = 129/302) of the RNAs that accumulated in the condensin mutant also accumulated in cells lacking Rrp6 (Figure 1G,H), with no clear preference for ncRNA and mRNA transcripts (50% each).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative RNA-seq analysis shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claims.claim: The overlap between RNAs accumulated in cut14-208 and rrp6Δ was statistically highly significant.
claims.source: A hypergeometric test confirmed that this overlap was statistically highly significant (p=4.6e−55).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from hypergeometric test analysis.

claims.claim: A large fraction of transcripts that accumulate when condensin is impaired are normally targeted by the ribonuclease Rrp6.
claims.source: These data indicate that a large fraction of the transcripts that accumulate when condensin is impaired are normally targeted by the ribonuclease Rrp6.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overlap analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Visual inspection of RNA-seq profile of cut14-208 revealed widespread increase of reads downstream of 3' ends of genes.
claims.source: Visual inspection of the RNA-seq profile of the cut14-208 mutant revealed a widespread increase of reads downstream of the 3' ends of genes, suggesting defects in the termination of transcription (for an example, see the hsp9 gene in Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from RNA-seq data visualization shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Dis3 and Rrp6 prevent the accumulation of read-through transcripts.
claims.source: Dis3 and Rrp6 have been reported to prevent the accumulation of read-through transcripts, although through possibly different mechanisms (Lemay et al., 2014; Zofall et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: 3'-extended hsp9 RNAs accumulate in fission yeast cells when Dis3 is impaired, and to a lesser extent when Rrp6 is lacking.
claims.source: Lemay et al. have shown that 3'-extended hsp9 RNAs accumulate in fission yeast cells when Dis3 is impaired, and to a lesser extent when Rrp6 is lacking (Lemay et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: cut14-208 mutant cells accumulated 3'-extended hsp9 RNA of the same length as cells depleted of Dis3 or Rrp6.
claims.source: Importantly, cut14-208 mutant cells accumulated 3'-extended hsp9 RNA of the same length as cells depleted of Dis3 or Rrp6.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from northern blot analysis.

claims.claim: Other condensin mutants (cut3-477 and cut14-180) also accumulated read-through hsp9 RNA.
claims.source: Moreover, other condensin mutants, such as cut3-477 and cut14-180, also accumulated read-through hsp9 RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which demonstrates that the accumulation of uncleaved, 3'-extended hsp9 transcripts is a feature of condensin inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from northern blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The accumulation of uncleaved, 3'-extended hsp9 transcripts is a feature of condensin inactivation.
claims.source: Moreover, other condensin mutants, such as cut3-477 and cut14-180, also accumulated read-through hsp9 RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which demonstrates that the accumulation of uncleaved, 3'-extended hsp9 transcripts is a feature of condensin inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data across multiple condensin mutants.

claims.claim: 489 transcripts were extended at their 3' ends in cut14-208 cells, mostly mRNAs and ncRNAs.
claims.source: Using these criteria, we identified 489 transcripts, mostly mRNAs and ncRNAs, which were extended at their 3' ends (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from systematic RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Read-through RNAs were polyadenylated.
claims.source: Oligo(dT)-primed RT-PCR showed that read-through RNAs were polyadenylated (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from oligo(dT)-primed RT-PCR shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: GO term analysis revealed no specific feature defining the population of read-through transcripts in cut14-208 cells.
claims.source: GO term analysis revealed no specific feature defining the population of read-through transcripts that accumulate in cut14-208 cells.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO term analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Only 111 of the 489 read-through transcripts were also up-regulated.
claims.source: Furthermore, only 111 of the 489 read-through transcripts were also up-regulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), which suggests that the 3'-extended RNAs were not the by-product of increased transcription.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The 3'-extended RNAs were not the by-product of increased transcription.
claims.source: Furthermore, only 111 of the 489 read-through transcripts were also up-regulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), which suggests that the 3'-extended RNAs were not the by-product of increased transcription.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: ChIP against transcriptionally active RNA Pol II revealed no increased occupancy downstream canonical TTS in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.source: In addition, ChIP against transcriptionally active RNA Pol II revealed no increased occupancy downstream canonical TTS in cut14-208 mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), in contrast to the transcription termination mutant pfs2-11 that we used as control (Wang et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from ChIP-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The termination of transcription remains largely effective in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.source: This result suggests that the termination of transcription remains largely effective in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from ChIP data.

claims.claim: 3'-extended transcripts in cut14-208 cells are unlikely to stem from increased transcription beyond the TTS.
claims.source: The 3'-extended transcripts that accumulate in cut14-208 cells are, therefore, unlikely to stem from an increased transcription beyond the TTS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ChIP and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Condensin and cohesin frequently, but not systematically, co-localise along chromosomes.
claims.source: Condensin and cohesin frequently, but not systematically, co-localise along chromosomes (Kim et al., 2016; Nakazawa et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The accumulation of cohesin at the 3' ends of co-transcribed convergent genes locally strengthens the termination of transcription.
claims.source: It has been proposed that the accumulation of cohesin at the 3' ends of co-transcribed convergent genes locally strengthens the termination of transcription (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a prior hypothesis supported by citation.

claims.claim: There is an enrichment for genes in a convergent orientation throughout the fission yeast genome (~62%).
claims.source: As previously observed (Schmidt et al., 2009), we found an enrichment for genes in a convergent orientation throughout the fission yeast genome (~62%, n = 4302/6986).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from genome annotation analysis, confirming prior observations.

claims.claim: Read-through transcripts in cut14-208 emanated mostly from genes oriented in tandem (53%) and slightly less from convergent genes (47%).
claims.source: In contrast, the read-through transcripts that accumulated in the cut14-208 mutant emanated mostly from genes oriented in tandem (53%, n = 259/489) and slightly less from convergent genes (47%, n = 230/489).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: No change in the localisation of cohesin was observed at genes with read-through transcripts or at up-regulated genes in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.source: We also analysed the localisation of cohesin in cut14-208 cells grown at the restrictive temperature, using ChIP against the SMC3Psm3 subunit of cohesin tagged with GFP. We observed no change in the localisation of Psm3-GFP neither at genes with read-through transcripts nor at up-regulated genes in cut14-28 mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from ChIP experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: No read-through RNAs were observed at nmt2, tea3, mei4, or pdt1 genes in cut14-208 background.
claims.source: Read-through transcripts have been detected at the nmt2, tea3, mei4 and pdt1 genes in cohesin mutant cells (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008). In sharp contrast, we observed no read-through RNAs at any of these four genes in a cut14-208 background (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, contrasting with prior research.

claims.claim: Cohesin binding to chromatin and cohesin-dependent transcription termination remain largely unaffected when condensin is impaired by cut14-208.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that both cohesin binding to chromatin and cohesin-dependent transcription termination remain largely unaffected when condensin is impaired by the cut14-208 mutation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ChIP and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: 622 read-through RNAs, mostly mRNAs and ncRNAs, were detected in rrp6Δ cells.
claims.source: We detected 622 read-through RNAs, again mostly mRNAs and ncRNAs, in the transcriptome of cells lacking Rrp6 (Figure 2E), which confirms previous reports (Lemay et al., 2014; Zofall et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2E, confirming prior research.

claims.claim: Pol II occupancy remained unchanged downstream the TTS of genes with read-through transcripts in rrp6Δ cells.
claims.source: Pol II occupancy remained unchanged downstream the TTS of genes with read-through transcripts in rrp6Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), consistent with the idea that Rrp6 is needed to eliminate read-though RNAs at the co- or post-transcriptional level (Zofall et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from ChIP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, consistent with prior research.

claims.claim: 50% of read-through RNAs that accumulated in rrp6Δ cells were also extended at their 3' ends in cut14-208 mutant.
claims.source: Importantly, 50% of the read-through RNAs that accumulated in cells lacking Rrp6 were also extended at their 3'ends in the cut14-208 mutant (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The function of Rrp6 might be affected in a cut14-208 background.
claims.source: This reinforces the idea that the function of Rrp6 might be affected in a cut14-208 background.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap of read-through transcripts.

claims.claim: The steady state level of the Rrp6 protein remained unchanged in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.source: The steady state level of the Rrp6 protein remained unchanged in cut14-208 mutant cells (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: No change was observed in the mRNA levels of RNA-exosome or TRAMP components in cut14-208 mutant by RNA-seq.
claims.source: Likewise, we observed no change by RNA-seq in the mRNA levels of RNA-exosome or TRAMP components in the condensin mutant (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: 3'-extended read-through transcripts accumulate upon condensin inactivation in fission yeast.
claims.source: Collectively, these data indicate that 3'-extended read-through transcripts accumulate upon condensin inactivation in fission yeast and that this accumulation might stem from defects in the processing of these transcripts by Rrp6.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: The accumulation of read-through transcripts might stem from defects in their processing by Rrp6.
claims.source: Collectively, these data indicate that 3'-extended read-through transcripts accumulate upon condensin inactivation in fission yeast and that this accumulation might stem from defects in the processing of these transcripts by Rrp6.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the data.

claims.claim: cdc10-129 single mutant and cdc10-129 cut14-208 double mutant cells completed S phase and progressed through G2 phase and mitosis with similar kinetics.
claims.source: FACScan analysis of DNA content and cytological observations revealed that cdc10-129 single mutant and cdc10-129 cut14-208 double mutant cells completed S phase (t = 30 min after release) and progressed through G2 phase (t = 60 min) and mitosis (t = 90 min) with similar kinetics (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from FACScan and cytological analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Chromosome segregation was impaired in the cut14-208 mutant background, as revealed by anaphase chromatin bridges.
claims.source: Chromosome segregation was impaired in the cut14-208 mutant background, as revealed by the appearance of anaphase chromatin bridges (Figure 3B, green line), which were subsequently severed by the septum upon mitotic exit, producing the CUT phenotype (Cells Untimely Torn) (Figure 3B, red line).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cytological analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: FACScan analysis revealed the appearance of aberrant karyotypes in post-mitotic cut14-208 cells.
claims.source: Accordingly, FACScan analysis revealed the appearance of aberrant karyotypes in post-mitotic cells (t = 120 and 180 min; Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from FACScan analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: No up-regulation of reporter RNAs was detected during G2 phase in synchronized cdc10-129 cut14-208 cells.
claims.source: Remarkably, we detected no up-regulation of any of the three reporter RNAs that we had selected from the pool of upregulated transcripts in cut14-208 mutants (Figure 1B) during G2 phase in synchronized cdc10-129 cut14-208 cells (t = 60 min, Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Reporter RNAs started to accumulate at t = 90 min and further increased at t = 120 min and 180 min, coinciding with accumulation of aneuploid post-mitotic cells.
claims.source: These RNAs started to accumulate, however, at t = 90 min and further increased at t = 120 min and 180 min (Figure 3C), coincidently with the accumulation of aneuploid post-mitotic cells.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3C, correlated with FACScan data.

claims.claim: Condensin is possibly required for proper gene expression during late mitosis or early G1 phase.
claims.source: This result suggests that condensin is possibly required for proper gene expression during late mitosis or early G1 phase.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the timing of RNA accumulation.

claims.claim: No up-regulation of reporter RNAs was observed at any time point when cut14-208 cells were arrested at G2/M transition.
claims.source: To validate these results, we repeated the RT-qPCR measurements by synchronously releasing cut14-208 cells from the early S phase block only 1 hr after shifting the temperature to 36°C and re-arrested them already at the G2/M transition using a cdc25-22 mutation (Figure 3D,E). In this time course experiment, we observed no up-regulation of the reporter RNAs at any time point (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: RNA levels remained unchanged after a sustained arrest in metaphase by depletion of Slp1.
claims.source: Similarly, RNA levels remained unchanged after a sustained arrest in metaphase at 36°C by depletion of the anaphase promoting complex (APC/C) activator Slp1 (Figure 3G–I).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figures 3G-I.

claims.claim: In fission yeast, the function of condensin is dispensable for gene regulation during S and G2 phases of the cell cycle.
claims.source: We conclude that, in fission yeast, the function of condensin is dispensable for gene regulation during S and G2 phases of the cell cycle, consistent with the finding that condensin is largely displaced from the nucleus during this time (Sutani et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple synchronization experiments, consistent with prior research.

claims.claim: Condensin in budding yeast remains bound to chromosomes throughout the cell cycle.
claims.source: Condensin in the budding yeast S. cerevisiae remains, in contrast, bound to chromosomes throughout the cell cycle (D'Ambrosio et al., 2008b), which is reminiscent to the continuous nuclear localization of the condensin II complex in metazoan cells.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Condensin localizes to chromosomes of budding yeast cells released synchronously from G1 arrest.
claims.source: We first confirmed that condensin localizes to chromosomes of cells released synchronously into the cell cycle from a G1 mating pheromone arrest (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from chromosome spreading and ChIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Condensin bound to chromosomes during G1 phase in budding yeast and its levels increased as cells passed through S and G2 phases.
claims.source: Chromosome spreading and ChIP showed that condensin bound to chromosomes already during G1 phase and that its levels on chromosomes increased as cells passed through S and G2 phases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from chromosome spreading and ChIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: TEV cleavage of the Brn1 subunit efficiently released condensin from chromosomes in budding yeast.
claims.source: To inactivate condensin in budding yeast, we proteolytically cleaved the kleisin (Brn1) subunit of the condensin ring by inducing expression of a site-specific protease from tobacco etch virus (TEV) using a galactose-inducible promoter, which efficiently released condensin from chromosomes (Cuylen et al., 2011), even during G1 phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from ChIP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, using a method from prior research.

claims.claim: Only 26 transcripts were differentially expressed by at least two-fold in G1 phase-arrested budding yeast cells after condensin cleavage.
claims.source: We then compared the transcriptome of G1 phase-arrested cells after condensin cleavage to cells with intact condensin (Figure 4A). Remarkably, solely 26 transcripts were differentially expressed by at least two-fold (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from tiling array analysis shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claims.claim: Only six genes displayed an up- or downregulation of two-fold or more when budding yeast cells were released from G1 arrest after Brn1 cleavage and re-arrested in M phase.
claims.source: To rule out that such minor effect on gene expression was not an artefact caused by the G1 phase arrest, we repeated the experiment, but this time released cells after Brn1 TEV cleavage from the G1 phase arrest and re-arrested them in the subsequent M phase by addition of the spindle poison nocodazole, before preparing RNA for transcriptome analysis (Figure 4C). In this experiment, only six genes displayed an up- or downregulation of two-fold or more (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from tiling array analysis shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claims.claim: Condensin inactivation by releasing the complex from chromosomes has no major effects on gene expression in budding yeast cells prevented from undergoing division.
claims.source: We conclude that condensin inactivation by releasing the complex from chromosomes has no major effects on the gene expression program of budding yeast cells when these cells are prevented from undergoing division.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from tiling array experiments in budding yeast.

claims.claim: Defects in chromosome segregation caused by condensin inactivation might be causally responsible for condensin-dependent gene deregulation.
claims.source: The fact that we observed changes in transcript levels in asynchronously dividing cut14-208 fission yeast mutant cells, but not in fission or budding yeast condensin mutants that are prevented from undergoing anaphase, raises the possibility that defects in chromosome segregation caused by condensin inactivation might be causally responsible for condensin-dependent gene deregulation.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from comparing results across different experimental conditions.

claims.claim: An increase in transcript levels was measured after mitotic exit and chromosome severing when cut14-208 cells were arrested at G2/M transition and then released.
claims.source: Indeed, when we arrested fission yeast cut14-208 cells at the G2/M transition using the analogue-sensitive Cdc2asM17 kinase (Aoi et al., 2014), shifted the temperature to 36°C and then released them from the arrest to complete mitosis, we measured an increase in transcript levels after mitotic exit and the severing of chromosomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: Mutation of separase (ptr4-1) or APC/C (cut9-665) resulted in chromosome missegregation and severing, as well as increased RNA levels.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5A, mutation of separase (ptr4-1) or of a subunit of the APC/C (cut9-665) resulted in chromosome missegregation and severing by the cytokinetic ring upon mitotic exit, as well as an increase in RNA levels, in a manner similar to cut14-208.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cytological analysis and RT-qPCR shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The amplitude of increase in RNA levels correlated with the frequency of chromosome cutting in different mutants.
claims.source: Moreover, the amplitude of the increase in RNA levels correlated with the frequency of chromosome cutting in the different mutants (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis of cytological and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Analysis of five additional condensin mutations confirmed the correlation between RNA increase and chromosome missegregation prevalence.
claims.source: The analysis of five additional condensin mutations of increasing prevalence of chromosome missegregation further confirmed this correlation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of multiple condensin mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E.

claims.claim: Double mutant cdc15-140 cut14-208 cells exhibited chromatin bridges during anaphase at 36°C.
claims.source: Double mutant cells cdc15-140 cut14-208 exhibited chromatin bridges during anaphase at 36°C (Figure 5B), which indicates that cdc15-140 did not suppress the chromosome segregation defect caused by the cut14-208 mutation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cytological analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: cdc15-140 did not suppress the chromosome segregation defect caused by cut14-208.
claims.source: Double mutant cells cdc15-140 cut14-208 exhibited chromatin bridges during anaphase at 36°C (Figure 5B), which indicates that cdc15-140 did not suppress the chromosome segregation defect caused by the cut14-208 mutation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from cytological observations.

claims.claim: Chromatin bridges were no longer severed upon mitotic exit in cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant cells.
claims.source: However, in the absence of a cytokinetic ring, these chromatin bridges were no longer severed upon mitotic exit.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cytological analysis.

claims.claim: The gain or loss of chromosomal fragments and production of post-mitotic cells with unbalanced karyotypes were suppressed when cytokinesis was prevented.
claims.source: As a consequence, the gain or loss of chromosomal fragments and the production of post-mitotic cells with unbalanced karyotypes were suppressed when cytokinesis was prevented (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from FACScan analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Approximately 98% of RNAs up-regulated in cut14-208 single mutant were no longer detected as differentially expressed in cut14-208 cdc15-140 double mutant.
claims.source: Remarkably, parallel RNA-seq analysis revealed that ~98% of the RNAs up-regulated in the cut14-208 single mutant were no-longer detected as differentially expressed in the cut14-208 cdc15-140 double mutant (Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: The production of read-through transcripts was suppressed by cdc15-140.
claims.source: The production of read-through transcripts was similarly suppressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: RNA levels remained increased in the cdc15-140 rrp6Δ mutant.
claims.source: Note that RNA levels remained increased in the cdc15-140 rrp6Δ mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), ruling out a potential compensatory effect of cdc15-140 on Rrp6 deficiency per se.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: cdc12-112 mutation equally restored normal gene expression in the cut14-208 genetic background.
claims.source: Finally, we found that cdc12-112, another mutation that also impairs cytokinesis (Chang et al., 1997), equally restored normal gene expression in the cut14-208 genetic background (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), which confirms that cytokinesis was a driving force for the gene deregulation exhibited by the cut14-208 mutant.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D, confirming the role of cytokinesis.

claims.claim: Cytokinesis is a driving force for gene deregulation exhibited by the cut14-208 mutant.
claims.source: Finally, we found that cdc12-112, another mutation that also impairs cytokinesis (Chang et al., 1997), equally restored normal gene expression in the cut14-208 genetic background (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), which confirms that cytokinesis was a driving force for the gene deregulation exhibited by the cut14-208 mutant.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with multiple cytokinesis mutants.

claims.claim: Changes in mRNA and ncRNA levels in cut14-208 cells are mostly, if not entirely, the consequence of chromosome cleavage during cytokinesis.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that changes in mRNA and ncRNA levels exhibited by cut14-208 condensin mutant cells are mostly, if not entirely, the consequence of chromosome cleavage during cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments with cytokinesis mutants.

claims.claim: The severing of chromosomes by the cytokinetic ring leads to DNA damage and formation of genomically unbalanced daughter cells.
claims.source: The severing of chromosomes by the cytokinetic ring leads not only to DNA damage, as revealed by the accumulation of sustained Rad22-GFP foci (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), but also to the formation of genomically unbalanced daughter cells, as shown by FACScan analysis of DNA contents (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from microscopy and FACScan analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Both DNA damage and genomic imbalance phenotypes coincide with the increase in RNA levels and are suppressed by cdc15-140.
claims.source: Both phenotypes coincide with the increase in RNA levels, and both are suppressed by cdc15-140 (Figure 5B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from multiple analyses shown in Figure 5B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: DNA damage induced by Camptothecin or Zeocin did not increase ncRNA or mRNA levels.
claims.source: The appearance of sustained Rad22-GFP foci in cells treated with Camptothecin or Zeocin confirmed the accumulation of DNA damage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). However, RT-qPCR revealed no increase in ncRNA or mRNA levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), arguing that DNA damage is not the main driver for gene deregulation in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from microscopy and RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: DNA damage is not the main driver for gene deregulation in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.source: The appearance of sustained Rad22-GFP foci in cells treated with Camptothecin or Zeocin confirmed the accumulation of DNA damage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). However, RT-qPCR revealed no increase in ncRNA or mRNA levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), arguing that DNA damage is not the main driver for gene deregulation in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from DNA damage experiments.

claims.claim: The mis6-302 mutation disrupts kinetochore assembly and leads to production of aneuploid post-mitotic cells.
claims.source: To test the impact of genomic imbalance on gene expression, we used the thermosensitive mis6-302 mutation which disrupts kinetochore assembly, and hence accurate chromosome segregation during anaphase, leading to the production of aneuploid post-mitotic cells (Saitoh et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the mis6-302 mutation supported by citation.

claims.claim: mis6-302 causes neither chromatin bridges nor a CUT phenotype.
claims.source: Note that mis6-302 causes neither chromatin bridges nor a CUT phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the phenotype of mis6-302.

claims.claim: FACScan analysis of mis6-302 cells confirmed the appearance of genomically unbalanced cells.
claims.source: FACScan analysis of mis6-302 cells grown at the restrictive temperature confirmed the appearance of genomically unbalanced cells (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from FACScan analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: RT-qPCR of four reporter RNAs revealed a similar increase in mis6-302 cells as in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.source: Remarkably, RT-qPCR of four reporter RNAs revealed a similar increase in mis6-302 cells as in cut14-208 mutant cells (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Chromosome missegregation during mitosis resulting from condensin inactivation can lead to gene deregulation.
claims.source: This argues that chromosome missegregation during mitosis, which results from condensin inactivation, can lead to gene deregulation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with mis6-302 and other mutants.

claims.claim: The expression of six different families of tRNAs is modestly increased in cut3-477 condensin mutant cells grown at 36°C.
claims.source: It has been reported that the expression of six different families of tRNAs, as measured by RT-PCR, is modestly increased in cut3-477 condensin mutant cells grown at the restrictive temperature of 36°C (Iwasaki et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: A clear increase in tRNA levels was observed in cut3-m26, cut14-90, and cut14-208 cells.
claims.source: Although we could not detect any significant change in tRNA levels in cut3-477 cells, we observed a clear increase in cut3-m26, cut14-90 and cut14-208 cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The increase in tRNA levels correlated with the frequency of chromosome missegregation and with the accumulation of mRNAs and ncRNAs.
claims.source: The increase correlated with the frequency of chromosome missegregation and with the accumulation of mRNAs and ncRNAs (compare with Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis of RT-qPCR and cytological data.

claims.claim: Preventing aneuploidy in cut14-208 mutant cells by cdc15-140 restored normal steady state levels of tRNAs.
claims.source: Importantly, preventing aneuploidy in cut14-208 mutant cells by using the cdc15-140 mutation restored a normal steady state level of these tRNAs (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Non-condensin mutations that disrupted chromosome segregation (ptr4-1, cut9-665, mis6-302) resulted in increased tRNA levels similar to cut14-208.
claims.source: Conversely, non-condensin mutations that disrupted chromosome segregation, such as ptr4-1, cut9-665 or mis6-302, resulted in a similar increase in tRNA levels as in cut14-208 (Figure 6C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: The effects of ptr4-1 and cut9-665 on tRNA levels were more comparable to cut14-208 than to mis6-302.
claims.source: We noticed, however, that the effects of ptr4-1 and cut9-665 were more comparable to the cut14-208 mutation than to the mis6-302 mutation, which did not upregulate the tRNAs SER +MET and THR (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The difference in tRNA upregulation between cut14-208 and mis6-302 is unlikely to be caused by DNA damage.
claims.source: This difference between cut14-208 and mis6-302 is unlikely to be caused by DNA damage that occurs in cut14-208 cells upon mitotic exit, as neither Camptothecin nor Zeocin treatment increased tRNA levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from DNA damage experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The difference in tRNA upregulation might be a manifestation of phenotypic variability associated with the aneuploid condition.
claims.source: It might rather be the manifestation of an inherent phenotypic variability associated with the aneuploid condition (Beach et al., 2017) (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claims.claim: The imbalance in genomic content from chromosome missegregation during mitosis is a major cause of deregulation of cellular RNAs when condensin is impaired.
claims.source: Nevertheless, taken together, these results strongly suggest that the imbalance in genomic content that results from chromosome missegregation during mitosis is a major cause of the deregulation of most, if not all, cellular RNAs when the function of condensin is impaired.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments with different mutants.

claims.claim: Condensin plays a major role in the segregation of the rDNA during late anaphase in budding yeast.
claims.source: It had been reported that condensin plays a major role in the segregation of the rDNA during late anaphase in budding yeast (Freeman et al., 2000; Sullivan et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citations.

claims.claim: Condensin plays a major role in the segregation of the rDNA during late anaphase in fission yeast.
claims.source: We reached the same conclusion in fission yeast, confirming previous observations (Nakazawa et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study confirming prior research.

claims.claim: Sister rDNA copies failed to separate during anaphase in cut14-208 mutant cells, frequently resulting in anucleolate daughter cells.
claims.source: When we scored the segregation of a GFP-labelled version of the rDNA-binding protein Gar2, we found that sister rDNA copies failed to separate during anaphase in cut14-208 mutant cells, frequently resulting in the formation of anucleolate daughter cells (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The ptr4-1 and mis6-302 mutants also exhibited a high rate of anucleolate cell formation.
claims.source: The ptr4-1 and mis6-302 mutants also exhibited a high rate of anucleolate cell formation (Figure 7A), whereas the cdc15-140 mutation suppressed the formation of anucleolate cells in the cut14-208 mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The cdc15-140 mutation suppressed the formation of anucleolate cells in the cut14-208 mutant.
claims.source: The ptr4-1 and mis6-302 mutants also exhibited a high rate of anucleolate cell formation (Figure 7A), whereas the cdc15-140 mutation suppressed the formation of anucleolate cells in the cut14-208 mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The inability to properly segregate the rDNA during anaphase correlates with the accumulation of mRNAs and ncRNAs targeted by the RNA-exosome.
claims.source: Thus, the inability to properly segregate the rDNA during anaphase correlates with the accumulation of mRNAs and ncRNAs targeted by the RNA-exosome.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from correlation of rDNA segregation and RNA accumulation data.

claims.claim: Rrp6 is enriched in the nucleolus and its amount was markedly reduced in cut14-208 anucleolate daughter cells.
claims.source: Co-immunostaining of Rrp6 tagged with a myc epitope and Gar2 tagged with GFP confirmed the nuclear localisation of Rrp6 and its marked enrichment within the nucleolus (Figure 7B). In a wild-type background, Rrp6 appeared evenly distributed between nuclei in post-mitotic daughter cells (median signal ratio ~1). In sharp contrast, the amount of Rrp6 was markedly reduced in cut14-208 anucleolate daughter cells compared to their nucleolate counterparts (median signal ratio ~0.25; Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: A similar asymmetric distribution of Dis3 was observed in post-mitotic cut14-208 cells.
claims.source: We observed a similar asymmetric distribution of Dis3 tagged with an HA epitope in post-mitotic cut14-208 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Residual levels of Rrp6 and Dis3 proteins remained detectable in anucleolate cells.
claims.source: Residual levels of Rrp6 and Dis3 proteins remained detectable in anucleolate cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), which suggests that a small fraction of Rrp6 and Dis3 molecules is transmitted to daughter cells independently of the rDNA.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: A small fraction of Rrp6 and Dis3 molecules is transmitted to daughter cells independently of the rDNA.
claims.source: Residual levels of Rrp6 and Dis3 proteins remained detectable in anucleolate cells (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), which suggests that a small fraction of Rrp6 and Dis3 molecules is transmitted to daughter cells independently of the rDNA.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila.
claims.source: Knowing that Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila (Graham et al., 2009), we propose that the bulk of Rrp6 and Dis3 might similarly co-segregate with the nucleolus in fission yeast, while a fraction is presumably transmitted to daughter cells in association with chromatin or within the nucleoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: The bulk of Rrp6 and Dis3 might co-segregate with the nucleolus in fission yeast, while a fraction is transmitted to daughter cells in association with chromatin or within the nucleoplasm.
claims.source: Knowing that Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila (Graham et al., 2009), we propose that the bulk of Rrp6 and Dis3 might similarly co-segregate with the nucleolus in fission yeast, while a fraction is presumably transmitted to daughter cells in association with chromatin or within the nucleoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on prior research and current findings.

claims.claim: The segregation of Dis3-mNeonGreen into daughter cells was severely impaired during the first cell division after condensin inactivation by Brn1 cleavage in budding yeast.
claims.source: Live cell imaging in budding yeast furthermore demonstrated that the segregation into the daughter cells of a mNeonGreen-tagged version of Dis3 was severely impaired during the first cell division after condensin inactivation by Brn1 cleavage (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from live cell imaging shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Condensin deficiency leads to rDNA non-disjunction during anaphase and production of anucleolate post-mitotic cells depleted of Rrp6 and Dis3.
claims.source: We conclude that condensin deficiency leads to rDNA non-disjunction during anaphase and the production of anucleolate post-mitotic cells, which are depleted of Rrp6 and Dis3.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: mug93as levels were considerably higher in cut14-208 mutant cells than in wild-type cells.
claims.source: Single molecule RNA-FISH showed that the ncRNA mug93as produced very faint signals in wild-type cells (Figure 7D), consistent with its active degradation by the RNA-exosome (Figure 1D). On the contrary, mug93as levels were considerably higher in cut14-208 mutant cells (Figure 7D), which confirms our previous RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from single molecule RNA-FISH shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: mug93as RNA accumulated mainly in anucleolate cells devoid of Gar2-GFP, with highest signals in anucleolate cells with low chromatin amount.
claims.source: Crucially, mug93as RNA accumulated mainly in anucleolate cells devoid of Gar2-GFP, with the highest signals in anucleolate cells with low chromatin amount, as judged by DAPI staining.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from single molecule RNA-FISH analysis.

claims.claim: A control mRNA (cct2) was evenly distributed between daughter cells in the cut14-208 mutant.
claims.source: In sharp contrast, a control mRNA (cct2) was evenly distributed between the daughter cells in the cut14-208 mutant (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from single molecule RNA-FISH shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Condensin loss-of-function leads to formation of anucleolate cells that accumulate RNA-exosome-sensitive transcripts.
claims.source: We conclude that condensin loss-of-function leads to the formation of anucleolate cells that accumulate RNA-exosome-sensitive transcripts.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from single molecule RNA-FISH and other data.

claims.claim: The functional integrity of condensin is dispensable for the maintenance of proper gene expression during interphase and mitosis in fission and budding yeasts.
claims.source: Here, we challenge the idea that condensin complexes directly regulate transcription by providing compelling evidence that the functional integrity of condensin is dispensable for the maintenance of proper gene expression during interphase and even mitosis in fission and budding yeasts.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: Condensin deficiency alters the transcriptome of post-mitotic cells in fission yeast, but this effect is mostly the indirect consequence of chromosome missegregation during anaphase.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies, we show that condensin deficiency alters the transcriptome of post-mitotic cells in fission yeast. However, this effect is mostly, if not entirely, the indirect consequence of chromosome missegregation during anaphase.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: Condensin plays no direct role in the control of gene expression in fission and budding yeasts, but is essential for maintaining proper gene expression by contributing to accurate chromosome segregation during mitosis.
claims.source: Our findings therefore indicate that condensin plays no direct role in the control of gene expression in fission and budding yeasts, but is essential for the maintenance of proper gene expression by contributing to the accurate segregation of chromosomes during mitosis.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: cut14-208 condensin mutant cells accumulate tRNAs, mRNAs, ncRNAs and 3'-extended read-through transcripts.
claims.source: Strand-specific RNA-seq and RT-qPCR analyses reveal that cut14-208 condensin mutant cells accumulate tRNAs, mRNAs, ncRNAs and 3'-extended read-through transcripts.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from RNA-seq and RT-qPCR analyses.

claims.claim: Other condensin mutants (cut3-m26, cut14-90, cut14-180) exhibit similar increases in RNA levels as cut14-208.
claims.source: Other condensin mutants such as cut3-m26, cut14-90 and cut14-180 exhibit similar increases in RNA levels, arguing that condensin takes part in proper gene expression in fission yeast, similar to other organisms.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis of multiple condensin mutants.

claims.claim: When cut14-208 cells were synchronised at S, G2 phase, or metaphase, RNA levels remained unchanged.
claims.source: However, when cut14-208 cells were synchronised at S or G2 phase or even at metaphase, RNA levels remained unchanged.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis of synchronized cells.

claims.claim: The suppressive effect of cdc15-140 upon cut14-208 on changes in gene expression argues that condensin impinges on gene expression in a cytokinesis-dependent manner.
claims.source: Moreover, the prevalent suppressive effect of cdc15-140 upon cut14-208 on changes in gene expression argues that condensin impinges on gene expression in a cytokinesis-dependent manner, and therefore in an indirect manner.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant.

claims.claim: Condensin deficiency makes no predominant impact on the steady state level of RNAs in post-mitotic cells by itself.
claims.source: Importantly, it also implies that condensin deficiency makes by itself no predominant impact on the steady state level of RNAs in post-mitotic cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the suppressive effect of cdc15-140.

claims.claim: Condensin plays no major direct role in the maintenance of proper gene expression during interphase or mitosis in fission yeast.
claims.source: Thus, although we cannot rule out the possibility that subtle impacts of condensin on the dynamics of transcription might have escaped our detection, our data strongly indicate that condensin plays no major direct role in the maintenance of proper gene expression during interphase or during mitosis in fission yeast.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple synchronization and genetic experiments.

claims.claim: Condensin is largely dispensable for the maintenance of gene expression programs during G1 phase or metaphase in budding yeast.
claims.source: Concordantly, we show that also in budding yeast, condensin is largely dispensable for the maintenance of gene expression programs during the G1 phase or during metaphase.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from tiling array experiments in budding yeast.

claims.claim: The separation of budding and fission yeast lineages is thought to have occurred ~420 million years ago.
claims.source: Note that the separation of the budding and fission yeast lineages is thought to have occurred ~420 million years ago, which makes them as distant from each other as either is from animals (Sipiczki, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast evolution supported by citation.

claims.claim: In two evolutionarily distant organisms (budding and fission yeast), condensin complexes play no major direct role in the maintenance of an established gene expression program.
claims.source: Thus, in two evolutionarily distant organisms, condensin complexes play no major direct role in the maintenance of an established gene expression program.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments in both yeast species.

claims.claim: The increased RNA levels in fission yeast cells defective for condensin are the indirect consequence of a failure during late mitosis caused by lack of condensin activity.
claims.source: The corollary is that the increased RNA levels exhibited by fission yeast cells defective for condensin must be the indirect consequence of a failure during late mitosis caused by a lack of condensin activity.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference drawn from the finding that condensin has no direct role in gene expression.

claims.claim: Suppressing the production of genetically unbalanced daughter cells by cdc15-140 is sufficient to restore an almost normal transcriptome despite condensin being impaired.
claims.source: Furthermore, suppressing the production of genetically unbalanced daughter cells by the cytokinesis mutation cdc15-140 is sufficient to restore an almost normal transcriptome, despite condensin being impaired by the cut14-208 mutation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis of cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant.

claims.claim: Preventing proper chromosome segregation by mutations in separase, APC/C, or kinetochore is sufficient to trigger accumulation of aberrant transcripts like in cut14-208 cells.
claims.source: Reciprocally, preventing proper chromosome segregation by mutations in separase (ptr4-1), the APC/C (cut9-665) or the kinetochore (mis6-302) is sufficient to trigger the accumulation of aberrant transcripts alike in cut14-208 cells.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RT-qPCR analysis of multiple mutants.

claims.claim: The missegregation of chromosomes during anaphase is the principal mechanism responsible for changes in RNA levels in condensin mutant cells.
claims.source: Therefore, the missegregation of chromosomes during anaphase appears to be the principal responsible mechanism for the changes in RNA levels exhibited by condensin mutant cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple genetic experiments.

claims.claim: Sister-rDNAs systematically fail to disjoin during anaphase in cut14-208 condensin mutant cells, leading to production of anucleolate daughter cells.
claims.source: Indeed, we show (1) that sister-rDNAs systematically fail to disjoin during anaphase in cut14-208 condensin mutant cells, leading to the production of anucleolate daughter cells;
claims.evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis.

claims.claim: Rrp6 and Dis3, which are enriched in the nucleolus, become depleted from anucleolate cut14-208 cells.
claims.source: (2) Rrp6 and Dis3, which are enriched in the nucleolus, become depleted from anucleolate cut14-208 cells;
claims.evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence analysis.

claims.claim: The reduction of Rrp6 and Dis3 from anucleolate condensin mutant cells coincides with increased steady state levels of RNA-exosome-sensitive transcripts.
claims.source: (3) the reduction of Rrp6 and Dis3 from anucleolate condensin mutant cells coincides with an increased steady state level of RNA-exosome-sensitive transcripts;
claims.evidence: This is a correlation observed from immunofluorescence and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The antisense RNA mug93as accumulates principally if not exclusively in anucleolate condensin mutant cells.
claims.source: and (4) an RNA-exosome sensitive transcript, the antisense RNA mug93as, accumulates principally if not exclusively in anucleolate condensin mutant cells, as expected from an impaired degradation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from single molecule RNA-FISH analysis.

claims.claim: Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila.
claims.source: Knowing that Rrp6 accumulates predominantly on chromosomes during mitosis in Drosophila (Graham et al., 2009), we propose that the bulk of Rrp6 and Dis3 might similarly co-segregate with the nucleolus in fission yeast, while a fraction is presumably transmitted to daughter cells in association with chromatin or within the nucleoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: The co-depletion of Rrp6 and Dis3 from anucleolate cut14-208 cells explains why the transcriptomes of cut14-208 and rrp6Δ strains overlap only partially.
claims.source: The co-depletion of Rrp6 and Dis3 from anucleolate cut14-208 cells provides a straightforward explanation as to why the transcriptomes of the cut14-208 and rrp6Δ strains overlap only partially, and to the slight additive effect exhibited by the cut14-208 and rrp6Δ mutations with respect to the accumulation of mug93as (Figure 1D) and of 3'-extented hsp9 RNA (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an explanation inferred from the co-depletion of both RNA-exosome components.

claims.claim: Condensin deficiency impairs chromosome segregation during anaphase, leading to chromatin bridges and rDNA non-disjunction.
claims.source: Condensin deficiency impairs chromosome segregation during anaphase, and notably leads to chromatin bridges and the non-disjunction of the rDNA.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from cytological analysis.

claims.claim: Upon mitotic exit, failure to properly segregate chromosomes alters the karyotype of daughter cells and creates an aneuploid condition that changes cellular RNA content.
claims.source: Upon mitotic exit, this failure to properly segregate chromosomes alters the karyotype of daughter cells and creates an aneuploid condition that changes the cellular RNA content.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from FACScan and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Rrp6 and Dis3 enriched in the nucleolus during mitosis become depleted from anucleolate daughter cells, reducing RNA-exosome activity.
claims.source: In particular, Rrp6 and Dis3 which are enriched in the nucleolus during mitosis become depleted from anucleolate daughter cells. This reduces the activity of the RNA-exosome, allowing the accumulation of RNA molecules that are normally actively degraded by the RNA-exosome, such as ncRNAs and 3'-extended RNAs.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation drawn from immunofluorescence and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Chromosome missegregation caused by condensin deficiency indirectly changes cellular RNA contents in fission yeast.
claims.source: This sequence of events illustrate how chromosome missegregation caused by condensin deficiency indirectly changes cellular RNA contents in fission yeast.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the mechanistic model.

claims.claim: Aneuploid cells exhibit gene-specific deregulations along a stereotypical 'aneuploid stress-response'.
claims.source: Aneuploid cells exhibit gene-specific deregulations along a more stereotypical 'aneuploid stress-response' characterised by an increased expression of genes involved in the response to stress and a down-regulation of cell-cycle and proliferation genes (Santaguida and Amon, 2015; Sheltzer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about aneuploidy supported by citations.

claims.claim: Premalignant murine T-cells defective for condensin II exhibit a transcriptome evocative of a stress response to aneuploidy.
claims.source: Premalignant murine T-cells defective for condensin II exhibit a transcriptome evocative of a stress response to aneuploidy (Woodward et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: Depletion of Smc2 in a human neuroblastoma cell line modifies expression of genes mainly involved in cell cycle progression or DNA damage response.
claims.source: Similarly, the depletion of Smc2, and hence the reduction of both condensin I and II, in a human neuroblastoma cell line modifies the expression of a large number of genes implicated mainly in cell cycle progression or DNA damage response (Murakami-Tonami et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: No clear transcriptomic signature of aneuploidy stress response was observed in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.source: However, we did not observed such a clear transcriptomic signature in cut14-208 mutant cells.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Condensin deficiency causes mostly severing of chromosome arms by the cytokinetic ring in fission yeast, leading to partial- or micro-aneuploidy.
claims.source: One possible explanation is that condensin deficiency causes mostly the severing of chromosome arms by the cytokinetic ring in fission yeast, which presumably leads to the gain or loss of chromosomal fragments rather than of entire chromosomes. The resulting partial- or micro-aneuploidy (Pfau and Amon, 2012) might, in contrast to a whole chromosomal aneuploidy, not elicit a robust aneuploidy stress response, which presumably stems from the concomitant change in number of many genes that have little impact when varied individually (Santaguida and Amon, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of aneuploidy stress response signature, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Different types of aneuploidy might have varying impacts on the transcriptome.
claims.source: That different types of aneuploidy might have varying impacts on the transcriptome might also explain the slight differences we observed between the tRNA contents of cut14-208 and mis6-302 mutant cells, which missegregate entire chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed differences between mutants.

claims.claim: Multiple mechanisms linked to chromosome instability and aberrant karyotypes likely concur to modify the transcriptome when condensin is defective.
claims.source: In any cases, multiple mechanisms linked to chromosome instability and the genesis of aberrant karyotypes most likely concur to modify the transcriptome when condensin is defective.
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion about the complexity of mechanisms involved.

claims.claim: The slight up-regulation of histone genes in cut14-208 mutant cells has been attributed to indirect stabilization of the transcription factor Ams2 during defective anaphase.
claims.source: For instance, the slight up-regulation of histone genes that we observed in cut14-208 mutant cells has previously been attributed to an indirect stabilization of the transcription factor Ams2 during defective anaphase (Kim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: Cohesin accumulates at intergenic regions flanked by co-transcribed convergent genes where it prevents transcription beyond canonical termination sites.
claims.source: Probably pushed by active RNA Pol II, cohesin accumulates at intergenic regions that are flanked by co-transcribed convergent genes, where it prevents transcription to proceed beyond canonical termination sites (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: In the case of unidirectional transcription, read-through RNAs are produced in a cohesin-independent manner.
claims.source: It is important to note that in the case of unidirectional transcription, read-through RNAs are produced in a cohesin–independent manner (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008), implying that cohesin plays the role of a roadblock for RNA polymerases specifically at the 3'ends of co-transcribed convergent genes.
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: Cohesin remains bound to chromatin in cut14-208 cells, including at convergent genes that exhibit read-through transcripts.
claims.source: Our observation that cohesin remains bound to chromatin in cut14-208 cells, including at convergent genes that exhibit read-through transcripts, plus the lack of any noticeable increase in Pol II occupancy, argue that condensin is unlikely to prevent read-thought transcripts through a same mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from ChIP experiments.

claims.claim: 43% of read-through RNAs originate from genes oriented in tandem in cut14-208 cells.
claims.source: The fact that 43% of read-through RNAs originate from genes oriented in tandem in cut14-208 cells further support this conclusion.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Besides cohesin-dependent termination, another pathway dependent upon condensin exists that prevents read-through transcripts.
claims.source: Thus, besides cohesin-dependent termination, another pathway dependent upon condensin must also exist that prevents read-through transcripts.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on read-through transcripts.

claims.claim: Condensin is unlikely to play a direct role in preventing read-through transcripts, since cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant cells no longer accumulate read-through RNAs.
claims.source: However, and crucially, condensin is unlikely to play a direct role in this second pathway, since cdc15-140 cut14-208 double mutant cells no longer accumulate read-through RNAs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from RNA-seq data of double mutant cells.

claims.claim: The lack of read-through RNAs in cdc15-140 cut14-208 cells suggests condensin is unlikely to exert any major roadblock effect on active RNA polymerases.
claims.source: Furthermore, given that cut14-208 reduces the binding of condensin to chromatin (Nakazawa et al., 2015), the lack of read-through RNAs in cdc15-140 cut14-208 cells suggests that condensin is unlikely to exert any major roadblock effect on active RNA polymerases.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from RNA-seq data and prior research on condensin binding.

claims.claim: The overlap between cut14-208 and rrp6Δ cells suggests it is the degradation of read-through transcripts that is impaired.
claims.source: The overlap between cut14-208 and rrp6Δ cells suggests instead that it is the degradation of read-through transcripts that is impaired.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Read-through transcripts are produced in wild-type cells.
claims.source: Read-through transcripts are produced in wild-type cells (Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008; Zofall et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Read-through RNAs are naturally produced at both tandem and convergent genes in wild-type cells but are rapidly degraded by Rrp6.
claims.source: We therefore propose that read-through RNAs are naturally produced both at tandem and convergent genes in wild-type cells, but are rapidly degraded by Rrp6.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claims.claim: Chromosome missegregation during mitosis caused by condensin deficiency induces accumulation of read-through transcripts by depleting Rrp6 from karyotypically abnormal daughter cells.
claims.source: Chromosome missegregation during mitosis caused by condensin deficiency induces their accumulation, despite the presence of cohesin, at least in part by depleting Rrp6 from karyotypically abnormal daughter cells.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claims.claim: Sister-rDNA almost systematically non-disjoin during anaphase in fission yeast condensin mutant cells.
claims.source: Our finding that sister-rDNA almost systematically non-disjoin during anaphase in fission yeast condensin mutant cells is consistent with the severe missegregation of the rDNA observed in budding yeast and human cells deprived of functional condensin complexes (D'Ambrosio et al., 2008b; Freeman et al., 2000; Samoshkin et al., 2012), and with the idea that decatenation of sister-rDNA during late anaphase relies upon condensin (D'Ambrosio et al., 2008a ).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the current study consistent with prior research.

claims.claim: The asymmetric partitioning of Dis3 in budding yeast daughter cells after condensin inactivation can be interpreted as a consequence of failure to disjoin sister-rDNA during anaphase.
claims.source: In that context, the asymmetric partitioning of the ribonuclease Dis3 that we observed in budding yeast daughter cells after the inactivation of condensin by TEV cleavage can be reasonably interpreted as a consequence of a failure to disjoin sister-rDNA during anaphase.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the live imaging data in budding yeast.

claims.claim: Mutations affecting condensin generate anucleolate cells that accumulate polyadenylated RNAs in budding yeast.
claims.source: In addition, it has been reported that mutations affecting condensin generate anucleolate cells that accumulate polyadenylated RNAs in budding yeast (Paul and Montpetit, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: The missegregation of the rDNA that occurs when condensin is impaired presumably impinges upon gene expression in budding yeast, like in fission yeast.
claims.source: Therefore, the missegregation of the rDNA that frequently occurs during anaphase when condensin is impaired presumably impinges upon gene expression in budding yeast, alike in fission yeast.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from findings in both yeast species.

claims.claim: Chromatin bridges are almost systematically severed by the cytokinetic ring in cut14-208 mutant cells, while severing of the nucleolus is extremely infrequent.
claims.source: One related aspect that remains puzzling, however, is that chromatin bridges are almost systematically severed by the cytokinetic ring in cut14-208 mutant cells, while the severing of the nucleolus is extremely infrequent (<10% of the cases).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from cytological analysis.

claims.claim: The persistence of the nucleolus in the axis of cleavage might mechanically hinder cytokinesis or trigger a wait signal.
claims.source: The persistence of the nucleolus in the axis of cleavage might mechanically hinder cytokinesis, or trigger a wait signal.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation.

claims.claim: Condensin deficiency might cause DNA double-strand breaks at fragile sites located on the centromere-proximal border of the rDNA cluster.
claims.source: Alternatively, condensin deficiency might cause DNA double-strand breaks at fragile sites located on the centromere-proximal border of the cluster of rDNA repeats, allowing the displacement of untangled sister-rDNA towards one pole of the mitotic spindle through a spring-relaxation effect.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation.

claims.claim: A focused role for condensin in organising a region proximal to the rDNA, located on its centromeric side, has been reported in budding yeast.
claims.source: A focused role for condensin in organising a region proximal to the rDNA, and located on its centromeric side, has been reported in budding yeast (Schalbetter et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is prior research finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: In HeLa cells, depletion of SMC2 induces DNA breaks predominantly in repetitive DNA, including the rDNA/Nucleolar Organising Regions.

claims.claim: Condensin loss of function might have similar confounding impacts on the preservation of structural integrity and proper expression of tandem repetitive DNA arrays in mammalian genomes.

claims.claim: The three-dimensional organisation of the genome influences gene expression.
claims.source: Studies performed over the past 20 years have shown that the three-dimensional organisation of the genome influences gene expression, raising the key question of the role played by SMC complexes in the control of gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.
